Russia is preparing for trilateral talks by launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s critical infrastructure. Repair and rescue operations are underway in the affected regions wherever the security situation allows. Nine people were injured, including one child.

I thank all our people who defend the country against this terror every day, work to restore what has been damaged, and do everything they can to get Ukraine through the winter. But when Russia is trying to plunge Kyiv – a city of millions – and the entire country into a blackout, Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on the U.S. Congress to give more attention to Ukraine, because Russia keeps increasing the number of its attacks. It is important that support for Ukraine remains among the priorities of U.S. policy. We are counting on both parties to stand united on matters of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin. America’s resolve and consistency in supporting Ukraine are crucial in bringing peace closer.

Republicans are blame-gaming each other, which can be constructive if over issues and reforms rather than social media ad hominem. But they need to message far better, about both the administration’s successes and the dangers of a socialist future.

There will be likely be no planned presidential succession, or gentlemanly agreement on a front runner. That’s likely good news. items.tx:
Today on November the 6th, our father, my mother's husband went home to be with his mother whom he lost when he was a young man. He also went to be with his father, whom he loved and respected immensely. 

Richard Neece Ojeda lived an extraordinary life. He enjoyed the love of a wonderful woman. He traveled the world and lived a life of service that started in the US Air Force and continued after graduating from the Mayo Clinic where he was commissioned as an officer in the US Army. 

After military service my father spent the next 55 years practicing anesthesia. He was the first man in Logan County history to perform an epidural at Logan Regional Hospital in Logan, WV. Over many years, he would be remembered as the man who gave the majority of epidurals for those giving birth in Logan County, West Virginia. 

My father enjoyed traveling to Guatemala where he worked with Doctors Without Borders and administered anesthesia to children born with cleft palates. On a normal trip to perform that work, he would treat over 1000 children every time he was there. 

Our father traveled the world. One of my favorite conversations with my father was in 1990, when I was stationed in Germany. I was at the train station in Frankfort when I called home. My father would tell me the details of that train station because he had also spent time there a couple of decades before me. In 2003, my father flew to South Korea to spend a couple of weeks with me where we climbed volcanoes in the South China Sea. We rode in a submarine and visited temples all across Cheju-Do Island. At the end of those two weeks, we both flew to Hawaii where we visited the USS Arizona at Pearl Harbor, visited Ernie Pyle's grave at the Punchbowl and climbed Diamond Head Peak in Honolulu. 

Our father was a very well-read man. He maintained a library in our home that is still in existence today. He was an avid supporter of scientists like Albert Einstein, Neal deGrasse Tyson and Carl Sagan and could spend hours talking about quarks and black holes. My father was a passionate Catholic and said his rosary almost every night. He was proud to be a member of the Knights of Columbus.........and my father was a very generous man. He gave freely. He loved everybody and believed that everyone deserved a second chance. He loved to ski and spent time skiing in Canada, Colorado and of course in the mountains of West Virginia. But most importantly, He loved his family. He spoke of his brothers and sisters often and was truly proud of each and every one of them. 

He would often speak about his brothers who all had reputations as being some of the best welders to work for the mines in southern West Virginia. His fondest memories go back to his childhood when he lived in the Coal Camp in Dehue, West Virginia. They didn't grow up with a lot of money.......but they were rich in love. His father taught every one of them the value of hard work while their mother showed them all how to be generous with those around them. If you were a child that was close to their home when it was dinner time, she fed them too. 

I could continue speaking the praises of my wonderful father. We will love him forever and live lives that will guarantee us all, that we will see him again.

Love you Pop ❤️

items.tx:
Abdul El-Sayed was five years old when he asked his grandfather Jan Johnson a question.

“Grandpa, how are you my grandpa?”

His grandparents-Jan and Judy had helped raise Abdul in Michigan, and until then Abdul had never had much reason to think about how they were related. But he had begun to notice that he looked nothing like either of them.

Abdul was 3 when his parents divorced. His father, Mohamed, later married Jackie Johnson, who helped raise him. Abdul called her Mom. So when he asked Jan how he could be his grandpa, Jan gave him a simple answer. Jackie was Jan’s daughter, and Jackie was Abdul’s mom. Then Jan added, “And because I love you.”

When Abdul was older, he spent summers with his father’s family in Alexandria, Egypt. His grandmother there was Soad. She cooked over a small burner with one pot, and Abdul loved to listen to her tell stories. At the end of the summer, he would go back to Michigan, to a cottage on a lake that had been in Jackie’s family for generations. He remembers trying to explain Soad to Grandma Judy. Even now, he says, it is hard to imagine either of his grandmothers knowing what to make of the other’s life.

Soad never got to go to school. She had eight children, and two of them died before their first birthdays. When Abdul talked about her as an adult, he still counted those two babies as the aunt and uncle he would have had. Soad used to remind him that he and his cousins in Egypt were no different from one another. He had simply been given chances they had not . As such, she expected him to do something with those opportunities.

Abdul thought about Soad years later when he began looking at how long people lived. By his reckoning, there was a gap of about ten years in life expectancy between the part of Michigan where he grew up and Egypt. But what bothered him was that he could find a gap about as large much closer to home. He could get on the freeway in suburban Oakland County, drive south into Detroit and see it in less than half an hour.

After medical school, Abdul took on the job of rebuilding Detroit’s health department.

Isitoshe, 

When Abdul ran for the U.S. Senate, Jan and Judy sat together in front of a camera. They told Michigan voters that they had helped raise him. Jan talked about how Abdul had helped children get eyeglasses through his work in public health. Then he mentioned something from their own life that had never been on the news. Their grandson still bought their groceries every week.

"It was obviously the Iran War. Trump didn't put America first. He betrayed America. It was gas prices. Only a fool would think otherwise."

Allow me to present a hypothetical scenario. Let's pretend that Trump #2 never started the war with Iran.

Imagine if the price of gas was not around $4.00 a gallon but instead, let's say something low, assume $2.70 a gallon.

Pretend inflation was at a near perfect 2% for the year and GDP was cruising along at a 15 year high.

Assume wages were up and unemployment was at about a 50 year low.

I shut down the conversation, but it was an extremely uncomfortable and depressing experience. What made it worse was that he was in the middle of cutting my hair. I couldn't simply get up and leave. 

I am so utterly sick of non-Jews presuming to tell Jews what Jew-hate is, what causes it and how we should understand our own experiences. The confidence with which some people dismiss Jewish experiences while insisting that their own understanding is more legitimate is astonishing.

I could not be more glad that I made Aliyah. Experiences like this remind me why I am so happy to call Israel home.

Shabbat Shalom. May we all find some peace this Shabbat.

items.tx: I worked as an election judge last Tuesday. This was my first time working an election, and I was shocked at how complicated the process is. While most people showed up with their TX driver's license and were registered to vote, a small but significant number of people required special attention... change in address, didn't show up in the system as registered, registered too late to vote, brought in a mail-in ballot and wanted to vote in person instead, brought an ID but not a Texas driver's license, paper got jammed in the ballot machine, didn't speak English... I was on the phone with HQ trying to sort these issues out all day long. Then the process to close the polls is incredibly complicated. Thankfully we had a trainer help us - it is not intuitive. I have new-found respect for the people who do this every election. It is hard work and long hours (5:30am start and I was lucky to get home at 10pm.)

items.tx:
I have known Chuck Schumer for 16 years. I worked closely with him and his staff when I worked for Harry Reid. I have a lot of respect for him and have also had my differences over the years. 

The job of leader happens mostly behind the scenes. The traits that make a good leader are not the same as what makes you good at social media, etc. Reid was famous for saying off-message stuff—lord knows how he would have fared in the age of social media. 

When you’re in the majority, the job is about setting the agenda and passing bills that help people. When you’re in the minority, you’re at the mercy of the majority in terms of the agenda, so the job is mainly to get back in the majority. 

By that measure, Schumer succeeded wildly on Tuesday. 

He oversaw the biggest Democratic sweep in the Senate since Watergate, recruiting candidates who fit their states and putting them in position to win states many had written off long ago. He was an early believer in Mississippi, for example. 

You can litigate this or that decision, and I certainly didn’t agree with them all—but when you step back and look at the big picture there’s simply no way to argue with this historic achievement. 

To me, the question of whether Schumer deserves to be reelected as leader after the most dominant performance by Senate Democrats in more than half a century is straightforward, and the answer is clearly yes.

Okay, I sat down and translated parts of yet another pompous statement from Jared Kushner about Trump’s incredible peace initiatives, explaining what his carefully worded euphemisms actually mean, so you don’t have to.

“…the need for a broader European security architecture that can help establish the conditions for lasting peace…”

= “Europe will have to completely capitulate to Putin, make him the master of the continent, and live under his dictates, because we’re absolutely itching to get our hands on Lukoil’s foreign assets.”

“For more than 30 years, Europe and Russia have struggled to establish a sustainable security framework.”

= “For decades, Europe and the entire West enjoyed peace and stability, until Putin, in his old age, suddenly got the itch to conquer Ukraine again, fucked it up spectacularly, and now somehow that’s everybody else’s problem.”

“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment.”

= “You will be required to surrender everything and remain defenseless, while Putin will give you absolutely nothing in return and won’t be obliged to do a damn thing.”

“Decades of mistrust, competing security concerns, and the devastating consequences of this war make this an extraordinarily difficult challenge, but one that is essential to lasting peace.”

= “And we’re also going to blame you and Ukraine for Russia’s aggressive imperialism.”

“Any arrangements must fully respect the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independent decision-making of every nation.”

= “And Putin will decide where your sovereignty begins and ends, where your borders lie, and just how much independence you’re allowed to have.”

“Each country will retain authority over its own security and alliances, and no country would have a veto over another’s sovereign choices.”

= “Yes, unless Putin decides that you’re not actually a real country at all, but an inseparable part of Russia’s sphere of influence, and that your ability to defend yourself against an invasion constitutes an existential threat to Russia.”

“We will consult closely with our European partners on the sidelines and, if progress is made, aim to move toward a broader multilateral format with their direct participation.”

= “Nobody is going to discuss a damn thing with Ukraine or Europe. There won’t be, and never has been, anything here except our attempts to sell out and betray you to Putin for the highest possible price. And I’ll throw in a whole bunch of meaningless, boilerplate diplomatic phrases to make this bullshit look vaguely serious and respectable.”

“There are no easy solutions.”

= “Russia could simply get the hell out of Ukraine and stop launching wars of aggression whenever it wants, but that’s not what Putin is promising us money for.”

“We will see how these discussions develop and continue working intensively with all parties toward President Trump’s objective of a comprehensive and lasting peace.”

= “Of course, absolutely nothing will come of any of this, just as nothing has come of all the previous years of these ridiculous ‘negotiations,’ during which we’ve been actively helping Putin wage his war. But we couldn’t care less. That’s not what we’re here for.”

I am not a full Q believer.

I have the unfortunate brain of believing in very little in general. A "trust, but verify" brain. Too many aspects of Q I can't verify.

I will entertain the idea of Q, which to many binary thinkers makes me a a believer in Q. I AM NOT.

Q is very easy to dismiss when viewed selectively. Elements are fuzzy. Can be dismissed as either a ball of yarn for conspiracy theorists or as a pacification campaign for patriots. I can entertain those possibilities. We are cooked if those are real. I would rather not. I choose hope.

Unequivocally, Trump is both aware of Q and posting Q related things. This can't be denied, or dismissed as horoscopes, it can only be dismissed through selection bias. It's very easy to prove, he hung this Q painting by @KAGdrogo at Trump National Golf Club in Los Angeles. This to me means A, that Q is real or B, he is pandering to his "trust the plan" followers. The B option would be tremendously cynical and cruel. Trump has never to my knowledge been cruel for cruel sake. I lean toward entertaining A, that Q is real.

We are not privileged with the bare naked truth yet, we are not Trump, we do not know what he is thinking. We don't know the full scope of Q yet. However, it is insane if 10% of the drops are true after all. Biggest military operation in history in both scope and scale.

Trump behaves very arrogantly. Arrogant people are either delusional, fake, or confident in their competence. To me Trump is the latter, confident in his competence. Like Kobe, or Jordan. Not arrogant, confident and competent at a level most can't comprehend. Which also leads me to entertain Q as real. If Q is real, Trump and very few others know the full plan. Susie Wiles doesn't know, Hegseth doesn't know, JD Vance doesn't know, they are all compartmentalized to a degree. Siloed. You can't blame JD for his post election post if he is not privy to the full Q plan. This also justifies Trump's position about JD Vance's post. Trump knows JD doesn't know. JD also didn't fully distance, chastise, or throw Trump under the bus, he merely stated, without malice, the facts that are available to him now.

Pundits who have long dismissed Q will have egg on their face if Q is real. Nick Fuentes stating he helped Democrats win, will look presumptuous if Democrats stole the election and are fully caught. As will Robert Barnes and Tucker Carlson. I don't blame them for their stances. They only have part of the story and have dismissed Q years ago. If Q is real, they are merely doing their best to make sense of the tangible parts of the story today.

You know what though, pundits don't matter if Q is real, because if Trump starts putting voting fraudsters in jail they will all come around very quickly.

Panicans are justified only if Q is anything but what it shows itself to be. Can you blame them for wanting more action? You certainly can't blame them for grasping for solutions or pointing fingers after Texas turned blue.

If Q isn't real, we are absolutely cooked. Communism and the DSA will infect the USA into it's grave in less than a decade. For the Q isn't real panican crowd who think we can get a majority again in 8-10 years haven't workshopped all the ways communists will build moats around that ever becoming a possibility. From stacking Scotus, killing our thought leaders with impunity, censoring us on every platform available, to infinite illegals and stuffed ballots. Under the DSA the American dream is dead.

If Q is real, its far grander of an undertaking than even the Manhattan project. Trump will look like a magician, a war general, and saint all wrapped into one. Imagine being that and not being a touch arrogant. Imagine how hard it was not to spill that full plan to people over the last 10 years. Imagine how humble he will look in retrospect.

Q will go down as the inverse of stabbing Caesar in the back. America could actually thrive another 250 years.

Trump will be looked at greater than Washingto

HRH Yasmine Pahlavi
Wife of HIH @PahlaviReza 
(The Leader of Iran’s Lion and Sun Revolution) :

Something deeply troubling is happening in Germany, and it should concern every person who values freedom.

This Saturday, my husband, Reza Pahlavi, will be in Frankfurt to accept the Freedom Prize on behalf of the people of Iran.

And yet, the Frankfurt police have officially informed us that we cannot attend or speak at the rally, and that they will prevent us from doing so.

Why?

Not because we have broken any laws. Not because we pose a danger to anyone.

But because the Islamic Republic has threatened violence against us.

The police have told us that if my husband attends, the Islamic Republic may retaliate by targeting innocent people in the crowd.

Think about that.

A foreign regime threatens violence against innocent civilians, and the response is to silence the very people it wants to intimidate.

Of course, protecting the lives of rally participants is essential. And I want to make something very clear: We have enormous respect and gratitude for the men and women in law enforcement who risk their lives every day to protect others.

But respecting law enforcement does not mean we cannot question a decision that appears to be driven by political considerations rather than security alone.

Because the fundamental question remains: Since when do threats of terrorism determine who is allowed to speak in a democracy?

This is precisely what it means to give in to terrorist threats.

In Germany. In a democracy. In a country where freedom of expression is a fundamental right.

If threats of violence are enough to silence us today, who will be silenced tomorrow?

The Islamic Republic has spent decades suppressing the voices of the Iranian people. Are we now going to allow its threats to dictate who can speak on German soil?

The Iranian people cannot freely assemble or speak without fear of persecution in their own country. That is precisely why our voices must be heard here.

We cannot allow the Islamic Republic to export its repression to Europe.

A democracy must protect its people from threats of violence, not surrender their freedoms to those making the threats
